target_customer: Startups and growth companies that hire contractors and employees internationally and need payroll and compliance
problem: In 2017 Pilot connected companies with vetted remote engineers and designers. It later moved into global payroll, contractor payments and employer of record services as Plane.
business_model: 2017: marketplace with a 30 percent fee over the contract. Now: per-worker payroll and EOR fees (for example $39 per contractor, $499 per EOR hire on the site).
product_category: HR tech, payroll and compliance (formerly remote contractor marketplace)

founders.name: Matt Pelc
founders.background_notes: Listed as Founder/CEO on the YC page.

founders.name: Matt Drozdzynski
previous_startups: Pilot (this company, started as a consultancy and dev shop)
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch, Feb 2017 names him as co-founder of Pilot. Whether this is the same person as Matt Pelc was not established.

competitors.name: Lystable
competitors.what: Contractor management platform software without its own marketplace

competitors.name: Hired
competitors.what: Recruiting marketplace focused mainly on screening, contrasted with Pilot by the founders

competitors.name: Large consultancies (Accenture, IBM, Infosys, Cognizant)
competitors.what: Provide contract engineering capacity to enterprises

technical_complexity.rationale: A curated marketplace with a matching algorithm and vetting is mostly operations and standard web engineering; the later payroll and compliance product is much harder.

defensibility.rationale: A marketplace of vetted contractors was copyable; the TechCrunch article notes long engagements (the longest four years) as the stickiness.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No acquisition found; the company changed business to global payroll and renamed itself Plane.

market_need_then: In Feb 2017 Pilot said it began as a dev shop with about 60 paid contractors, had been profitable, and pivoted to a marketplace after its own data showed unmet demand from clients including Lonely Planet.

branding.domain_note: Now uses plane.com; Pilot.co pages redirect to plane.com per a Plane blog post seen in search. Acquisition date and price not found.

identity.voice_and_tone: Developer and agent friendly, stresses open API, MCP and CLI

rebrands.why: Not found. Pilot.com (bookkeeping, a separate company) shares the earlier name.

brand_strength.rationale: Plane owns a short exact .com but shares its name with an open-source project management tool (plane.so) and Pilot was shared with a bookkeeping company, creating confusion.

pivots.from: Consultancy and dev shop with about 60 paid contractors
pivots.to: Curated remote freelance marketplace for engineers and designers
pivots.why: Operational data showed unmet demand, per TechCrunch Feb 2017 (about a year and a half before)

pivots.to: Global payroll, contractor payments and employer of record (Plane)
pivots.why: Not stated in sources found; date not found

outcome_analysis: Pilot began as a profitable dev shop and moved to a marketplace shortly before YC. It remains active about 30 people strong after changing its product to global payroll and renaming itself Plane. No funding round, valuation or exit could be verified, so how strong the traction is remains unclear.
notes: Seedtable (aggregator, not opened) lists a $1.1M seed around 2017-03 for Plane previously Pilot; kept out of rounds as single-source. A Polish outlet snippet names Staszek Kolarzowski as a Pilot founder; not opened so not listed. Pilot.com (bookkeeping, Index Ventures Series A 2018) and Plane (plane.so, open source PM tool, $4M seed 2023) are different companies. The YC page says founded 2017; TechCrunch says Pilot was about six years old in Feb 2017. The rename blog post returned HTTP 503.
